subject: maths
title: Comparing data sets
summary: Learn to compare two data sets using the mean, median and range, read back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots, and decide how outliers affect your comparison.
body:
Is one cricket team’s batting better than another’s? Did a new study method improve test marks? Is Melbourne warmer in March than in November? To answer questions like these you have to **compare two data sets** — and a single number, like the highest score, can easily mislead you. This lesson shows how to compare fairly using a centre, a spread and a good display.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can compare two data sets using a measure of centre (mean or median) and a measure of spread (range), read and use back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots, explain how an outlier affects the mean and median, and write a clear comparison sentence.

## Before you start

You need the mean, median, mode and range from *Mean, median, mode and range (Year 7)* and stem-and-leaf plots and dot plots from *Displaying data (Year 7)*.

**Warm-up**

1. Find the median of 4, 9, 2, 7. *(Answer: in order 2, 4, 7, 9, so (4 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.5)*
2. Find the range of 4, 9, 2, 7. *(Answer: 9 − 2 = 7)*

## Think of it like this

### Choosing between two archers

Two archers each shoot eight arrows. One archer’s arrows are all tightly bunched just above the bullseye. The other’s arrows are scattered all over the target, but their average position is right on the bullseye. To describe each archer you need two things: **where** the arrows land on average (the centre) and **how bunched** they are (the spread).

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a target is two-dimensional, but most data sets are just a list of numbers on a line — the "spread" is simply how far apart the smallest and largest values are.

## Key ideas

### Centre and spread

Every comparison should talk about two features:

- **Centre** — a typical value. Use the **mean** or the **median**.
- **Spread** — how far apart the values are. In Year 8 we use the **range** (largest − smallest).

A smaller range means the data is more **consistent** (the values are closer together). Two data sets can have the same mean but very different spreads.

### Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots

A **back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot** shows two data sets on one shared stem. One set’s leaves go to the right; the other’s go to the left. Leaves on the left are read from the stem outwards, so the smallest leaf is next to the stem. With one key, such as "2 | 4 means 24", you can see at a glance which set sits higher and which is more spread out.

| Class R leaves | Stem | Class B leaves |
|---|---|---|
| 8 5 2 | 1 | 9 |
| 7 6 4 3 1 | 2 | 2 5 5 8 |
| 4 0 | 3 | 1 3 6 8 |
|  | 4 | 3 |

Key: 2 | 4 means 24.

**Parallel dot plots** (two dot plots on the same scale, one above the other) do the same job for small data sets.

### Outliers and which centre to use

An **outlier** is a value far from the rest. It drags the mean towards it but hardly moves the median. So:

- With no outliers, compare **means** (they use every value).
- With an outlier, compare **medians**, and mention the outlier.

Removing an outlier usually makes a big difference to the mean and range, and only a small difference to the median.

### Writing a comparison

A good comparison names both data sets, gives the numbers, and says what they mean in context:

*"Class B’s median score (29.5) is higher than Class R’s (23.5), so Class B generally scored higher. The ranges are similar (24 and 22), so both classes were about equally spread out."*

Avoid comparing just the single highest or lowest values — one person doesn’t describe a whole group.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Two netball shooters scored these goals in 8 games.
Ana: 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9. Bree: 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 10, 10. Compare them.

![Parallel dot plots of goals in 8 games: Ana’s dots are bunched from 6 to 9; Bree’s are spread from 3 to 10](/diagrams/y8/maths/comparing-data-sets-ex1.svg)


Step 1: totals — Ana 62, Bree 62 — so both means are 62 ÷ 8 = **7.75** goals.
Step 2: medians (8 values, so average the 4th and 5th) — Ana (8 + 8) ÷ 2 = **8**; Bree (8 + 9) ÷ 2 = **8.5**.
Step 3: ranges — Ana 9 − 6 = **3**; Bree 10 − 3 = **7** — to measure spread.
Step 4: conclusion — they score about the same on average, but Ana is much more consistent (smaller range).

### Example 2

Use the back-to-back plot in Key ideas (quiz scores out of 50). Compare Class R and Class B.

Step 1: read Class R (left, from the stem outwards): 12, 15, 18, 21, 23, 24, 26, 27, 30, 34. Class B: 19, 22, 25, 25, 28, 31, 33, 36, 38, 43.
Step 2: means — Class R 230 ÷ 10 = **23**; Class B 300 ÷ 10 = **30**.
Step 3: medians (average of 5th and 6th) — Class R (23 + 24) ÷ 2 = **23.5**; Class B (28 + 31) ÷ 2 = **29.5**.
Step 4: ranges — Class R 34 − 12 = **22**; Class B 43 − 19 = **24**.
Step 5: conclusion — Class B generally scored higher (higher mean and median); the spreads are similar.

### Example 3

Minutes taken to finish a puzzle. Group S: 42, 45, 45, 48, 50, 52, 95. Group T: 47, 49, 50, 51, 53, 54, 56. Which group was generally faster?

![Parallel dot plots of puzzle times: Group S has six dots between 42 and 52 and one far away at 95; Group T has dots from 47 to 56](/diagrams/y8/maths/comparing-data-sets-ex3.svg)


Step 1: means — S: 377 ÷ 7 ≈ **53.9**; T: 360 ÷ 7 ≈ **51.4**. This makes S look slower.
Step 2: notice 95 is an outlier in S — it drags S’s mean up.
Step 3: medians (4th value) — S: **48**; T: **51**. So the typical S time is lower.
Step 4: conclusion — compare medians because of the outlier: Group S was generally faster, but one person in S took much longer.
Check: without 95, S has mean 282 ÷ 6 = 47 and median 46.5 — the mean dropped by almost 7, the median by only 1.5 ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Comparing only the biggest values.** One high score doesn’t make a group better. Fix: compare a centre and a spread.
- **Thinking a bigger range is better.** It just means more spread out. Fix: smaller range = more consistent.
- **Reading left-hand leaves backwards.** 1 | 7 on the left side is still 17, not 71. Fix: stem first, then leaf, on both sides.
- **Using the mean when there’s an outlier.** Fix: spot outliers first; if there is one, compare medians.
- **Averaging two means from groups of different sizes.** Fix: find each group’s total, add the totals, then divide by the total number of values.

## Tips to remember

- **"Middle and spread, then what it said."** Give a centre, a spread, then a sentence in context. (A made-up memory trick.)
- **Small range = steady hands.** Like an archer whose arrows are bunched.
- **Outliers push the mean, not the median.** Picture one heavy person on a seesaw tipping the mean.
- **Back-to-back: both read from the stem out.**
- **Same mean ≠ same data.** Always check the spread too.

## Key terms

- **Measure of centre** — a single typical value: the mean or median (or mode).
- **Measure of spread** — how spread out the values are; in Year 8, the range.
- **Range** — largest value − smallest value.
- **Consistent** — values close together (small spread).
- **Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot** — two data sets sharing one stem, with leaves on each side.
- **Parallel dot plots** — two dot plots on the same scale, one above the other.
- **Outlier** — a value much larger or smaller than the rest.

## Summary

- Compare data sets using a centre (mean or median) AND a spread (range).
- A smaller range means more consistent data.
- Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots and parallel dot plots show two data sets side by side.
- An outlier changes the mean a lot but the median only a little, so use the median when there’s an outlier.
- Finish with a clear sentence in context that uses the numbers.

questions.prompt: Two students recorded how many hours of homework they did on five school nights (shown in the dot plots). Jake: 3, 8, 5, 10, 4. Priya: 6, 7, 6, 5, 7. Whose homework times are more consistent?

options.A: Jake, because his range is larger (7 compared with 2)
options.B: Jake, because his largest value (10) is bigger
options.C: Priya, because her range is smaller (2 compared with 7)
options.D: They are equally consistent, because both have 5 values

questions.explanation: Jake’s range is 10 − 3 = 7 and Priya’s is 7 − 5 = 2. A smaller range means the values are closer together, so Priya is more consistent. A larger range means less consistent, not more.
steps: Jake: range = 10 − 3 = 7. Priya: range = 7 − 5 = 2.
More consistent means less spread out, so the smaller range wins: Priya.

mistakes.A: Step 2: a LARGER range means the values are more spread out, which is less consistent.
mistakes.B: Step 1: consistency is about spread, not about the biggest value. Work out each range.
mistakes.D: Step 1: having the same number of values does not tell you about spread. Compare the ranges.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of homework hours: Jake has dots at 3, 4, 5, 8 and 10; Priya has dots at 5, 6, 6, 7 and 7

questions.prompt:
Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot of daily maximum temperatures (key: 1 | 2 means 12 °C). Town X leaves are on the left and Town Y leaves are on the right.
Town X | stem | Town Y
7 5 2 | 1 | 3 6
4 1 | 2 | 0 2 5
What are Town X’s temperatures?
questions.explanation: Town X’s leaves are on the left, read outwards from the stem: stem 1 has leaves 2, 5, 7 (12, 15, 17) and stem 2 has leaves 1, 4 (21, 24). Writing 71 puts the leaf first — the stem is always the tens digit.
steps: Town X is on the left of the stem. Its leaves are read from the stem outwards (right to left), so they go from smallest to largest.
Stem 1, leaves 2, 5, 7 → 12, 15, 17. Stem 2, leaves 1, 4 → 21, 24.

mistakes.B: Step 1: you included the leaves on both sides. Only the leaves on the left belong to Town X.
mistakes.C: Step 1: these are the leaves on the right — they belong to Town Y. Town X’s leaves are on the left of the stem.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the stem is the tens digit for both towns. Put the stem first, then the leaf: stem 1 with leaf 7 is 17.

questions.prompt: Which pair of statistics is best for comparing how spread out two data sets are and where their middle is?

options.A: The mode for the middle, and the mean for the spread
options.B: The range for the middle, and the median for the spread
options.C: The largest value for the middle, and the smallest value for the spread
options.D: The median (or mean) for the middle, and the range for the spread

questions.explanation: To compare data sets, compare a measure of centre (mean or median) and a measure of spread (range). Swapping them is the usual slip: the range tells you spread, not the middle.
steps: Centre (the typical value): mean or median.
Spread (how far apart the values are): range.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the mean measures centre, not spread. Spread is measured by the range.
mistakes.B: Step 1: these are swapped. The range is a measure of spread; the median is a measure of centre.
mistakes.C: Step 1: single values don’t describe a whole data set. Use a measure of centre and a measure of spread.

questions.prompt:
Six test scores for each of two classes:
Class P: 65, 70, 72, 75, 78, 80
Class Q: 55, 68, 74, 76, 82, 95
Which statement is correct?

options.A: Class P has the higher median and the larger range
options.B: Class Q has the higher median and the larger range
options.C: Class Q has the higher median and the smaller range
options.D: The classes have the same median

questions.explanation: Medians: P = (72 + 75) ÷ 2 = 73.5 and Q = (74 + 76) ÷ 2 = 75, so Q is higher. Ranges: P = 80 − 65 = 15 and Q = 95 − 55 = 40, so Q is also more spread out — not less.
steps: Class P median = (72 + 75) ÷ 2 = 73.5; Class Q median = (74 + 76) ÷ 2 = 75.
Class P range = 80 − 65 = 15; Class Q range = 95 − 55 = 40.
So Class Q has the higher median AND the larger range.

mistakes.A: Step 1: work out both medians — P is (72 + 75) ÷ 2 = 73.5 and Q is (74 + 76) ÷ 2 = 75. Then compare the ranges.
mistakes.C: Step 2: Class Q’s range is 95 − 55 = 40, which is larger than Class P’s 15.
mistakes.D: Step 1: with six values, the median is halfway between the 3rd and 4th values. Work it out for each class.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of test scores: Class P has dots at 65, 70, 72, 75, 78 and 80; Class Q has dots at 55, 68, 74, 76, 82 and 95

questions.prompt: The ages of six people at a café table are 14, 15, 15, 16, 18 and 42. Which measure gives the best idea of a typical age, and what is it?
questions.explanation: 42 is an outlier, which pulls the mean up to 20 — older than five of the six people. The median, (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5, is not affected much, so it describes a typical age better.
steps: Notice the outlier: 42 is far from the other ages.
An outlier drags the mean, so use the median.
Six values, so the median = (3rd + 4th) ÷ 2 = (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the mean is 20, but the outlier 42 drags it above five of the six ages. With an outlier, use the median.
mistakes.C: Step 2: with six values the median is halfway between the 3rd and 4th values: (15 + 16) ÷ 2.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the range measures spread, not a typical value. Use a measure of centre.

questions.diagram_alt: Dot plot of ages: dots at 14, 15, 15, 16 and 18, and one dot far away at 42

questions.prompt: The data set 20, 22, 23, 25, 30 has a mean of 24 and a median of 23. The value 60 is added. What happens?

options.A: The mean rises to 30 and the median stays at 23
options.B: The mean rises to 42 and the median rises to 24
options.C: Neither changes, because 60 is an outlier
options.D: The mean rises to 30 and the median rises to 24

questions.explanation: New total = 120 + 60 = 180, and 180 ÷ 6 = 30. New median = (23 + 25) ÷ 2 = 24. The outlier moved the mean by 6 but the median by only 1 — it does still change, though.
steps: Old total = 24 × 5 = 120, so the new total = 120 + 60 = 180.
New mean = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.

mistakes.A: Step 3: adding a value changes the middle position. With six values, the median is halfway between the 3rd and 4th values.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you averaged the old mean and 60. Add 60 to the total (120) and divide by 6 values.
mistakes.C: Step 1: outliers are still part of the data. Recalculate the mean and median with 60 included.

questions.prompt:
Back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot of minutes taken to finish a puzzle (key: 3 | 1 means 31 minutes). Group 1 leaves on the left, Group 2 leaves on the right.
8 3 1 | 3 | 6 8 9
7 5 2 0 | 4 | 1 1 3 4 6
2 | 5 |
Which statement is correct?

options.A: The groups have the same median, but Group 2’s times are less spread out
options.B: Group 1 is faster, because its smallest time is lower
options.C: The groups have the same median and the same range
options.D: Group 2 has a higher median, because more of its leaves are in the 40s

questions.explanation: Group 1: 31, 33, 38, 40, 42, 45, 47, 52 — median (40 + 42) ÷ 2 = 41, range 21. Group 2: 36, 38, 39, 41, 41, 43, 44, 46 — median 41, range 10. Same centre, but Group 2 is more consistent.
steps: Group 1 (read the left leaves from the stem outwards): 31, 33, 38, 40, 42, 45, 47, 52. Group 2: 36, 38, 39, 41, 41, 43, 44, 46.
Medians (8 values, so average the 4th and 5th): Group 1 = (40 + 42) ÷ 2 = 41; Group 2 = (41 + 41) ÷ 2 = 41.
Ranges: Group 1 = 52 − 31 = 21; Group 2 = 46 − 36 = 10. Same median, but Group 2 is less spread out.

mistakes.B: Step 1: one fast person does not make a group faster. Compare the medians (both 41).
mistakes.C: Step 2: Group 1’s range is 52 − 31 = 21 but Group 2’s is 46 − 36 = 10.
mistakes.D: Step 2: having more leaves in the 40s does not decide the median. List each group in order and average the 4th and 5th values.

questions.prompt: In a survey, 15 Year 7 students did a mean of 12 minutes of reading a day, and 20 Year 8 students did a mean of 15 minutes a day. What is the mean for all 35 students, correct to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Totals: 15 × 12 = 180 and 20 × 15 = 300, so 480 minutes for 35 students, and 480 ÷ 35 ≈ 13.7. Just averaging 12 and 15 gives 13.5, which ignores that the Year 8 group is bigger.
steps: Year 7 total = 15 × 12 = 180 minutes.
Year 8 total = 20 × 15 = 300 minutes.
Combined mean = (180 + 300) ÷ 35 = 480 ÷ 35 ≈ 13.7 minutes.

mistakes.A: Step 3: averaging 12 and 15 ignores that the groups are different sizes. Find each group’s total minutes first.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 12 + 15 adds the two means. Means of groups can’t be added — combine the totals instead.
mistakes.D: Steps 1 and 2: you multiplied each mean by the other group’s size. Year 7 is 15 students × 12 minutes; Year 8 is 20 students × 15 minutes.

questions.prompt:
A coach must pick one player for a game where she needs reliable scoring. Points scored in the last 8 games:
Kira: 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13
Leah: 4, 6, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 17
Which choice and reason is best?

options.A: Kira: her mean is only 0.5 lower than Leah’s, but her range is much smaller (5 compared with 13)
options.B: Leah: her mean is higher, so she is always the better scorer
options.C: Leah: her range is larger, so she is more reliable
options.D: Kira: her mean is higher than Leah’s

questions.explanation: Kira: total 84, mean 10.5, range 5. Leah: total 88, mean 11, range 13. The means are close, but Kira is far more consistent, which is what “reliable” asks for. A larger range means less reliable.
steps: Kira: total 84, mean 84 ÷ 8 = 10.5, range 13 − 8 = 5.
Leah: total 88, mean 88 ÷ 8 = 11, range 17 − 4 = 13.
The means are almost the same, but Kira’s much smaller range makes her more reliable — choose Kira.

mistakes.B: Step 2: a slightly higher mean doesn’t mean "always" — Leah scored only 4 and 6 in two games. Look at the spread too.
mistakes.C: Step 2: a larger range means LESS consistent. Reliable means a small range.
mistakes.D: Step 1: check the means — Kira 84 ÷ 8 = 10.5, Leah 88 ÷ 8 = 11. Kira’s is lower.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of points: Kira’s dots are bunched from 8 to 13; Leah’s are spread from 4 to 17

questions.prompt: Data set M is 4, 7, 9, 11 and one more value, x, which is the largest value in the set. The mean of set M is 9. What is the range of set M?
questions.explanation: Total = 9 × 5 = 45, so x = 45 − (4 + 7 + 9 + 11) = 45 − 31 = 14. Range = 14 − 4 = 10. Giving 14 stops one step early — that is x, not the range.
steps: A mean of 9 for 5 values means the total is 9 × 5 = 45.
Range = largest − smallest = 14 − 4 = 10.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 14 is the value of x. The range is the largest value minus the smallest: subtract 4.
mistakes.B: Step 2: x is not 9 — the mean is the total divided by 5, so the total must be 9 × 5 = 45.
mistakes.C: Step 3: the range uses the smallest value, 4, not 7. Range = largest − smallest.

questions.prompt: The data set 3, 5, 6, 8, 13 has a mean of 7 and a median of 6. Which change keeps the mean at 7 but changes the median?

options.B: Change the 6 and the 8 both to 7
options.C: Change the 3 to 2 and the 13 to 14
options.D: Add the value 6 to the set

questions.explanation: Changing 6 and 8 to 7 and 7 keeps the total at 35 (mean 7) and makes the middle value 7. Changing 3 → 2 and 13 → 14 also keeps the mean, but only the end values move, so the median stays 6.
steps: To keep the mean at 7, the total of the 5 values must stay 35.
To change the median, the middle (3rd) value must change.
Changing 6 and 8 to 7 and 7 keeps the total at 35, and the new data 3, 5, 7, 7, 13 has median 7 — this is the one that works.

mistakes.A: Step 1: this adds 10 to the total, so the mean changes (to 9). The median stays at 6.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the total stays 35, so the mean is still 7 — but the middle value is still 6, so the median doesn’t change.
mistakes.D: Step 1: adding 6 makes the total 41 over 6 values, so the mean is no longer 7. Check each option’s total and middle value.

questions.prompt:
Heart rates (beats per minute) of 8 students before a test:
Group A: 52, 55, 58, 60, 61, 64, 65, 69
Group B: 48, 50, 53, 56, 62, 66, 70, 75
Tom says: "Group B has the highest heart rate, so Group B’s heart rates are generally higher." What is the best response?

options.A: Tom is right, because 75 is the highest value in either group
options.B: Tom is right, because Group B has the larger range
options.C: Tom is wrong: Group A has the higher mean and median; Group B only has more spread
options.D: Tom is wrong: Group A has the larger range

questions.explanation: Group A: mean 484 ÷ 8 = 60.5, median (60 + 61) ÷ 2 = 60.5, range 17. Group B: mean 480 ÷ 8 = 60, median (56 + 62) ÷ 2 = 59, range 27. A is slightly higher in the centre; B just has more extreme values. The highest single value is not a fair comparison.
steps: Group A: total 484, mean 60.5; median (60 + 61) ÷ 2 = 60.5.
Group B: total 480, mean 60; median (56 + 62) ÷ 2 = 59.
Ranges: A = 17, B = 27. Group A is a little higher in the middle; Group B is just more spread out — so Tom is wrong.

mistakes.A: Step 1: one large value doesn’t describe a whole group. Compare the means or medians.
mistakes.B: Step 3: a larger range means more spread, not higher values. Compare the centres.
mistakes.D: Step 3: Group A’s range is 69 − 52 = 17, which is smaller than Group B’s 27.

questions.diagram_alt: Parallel dot plots of heart rates: Group A from 52 to 69 and Group B from 48 to 75
